#3487. Netflix Officially Revives Sylvester Stallone’s Beloved Action Thriller Before the Remake

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

2026 has been a very good year to be a Sylvester Stallone fan. I Play Rocky, the story of how Stallone wrote the Rocky screenplay and bet everything on himself to play the lead against impossible odds, recently premiered at TIFF and is already being hailed as one of the best movies in an already stacked year. Then Stallone fans got another treat as well, when he revealed that he has completed the script for Rocky 7. Apart from the Rocky universe, Stallone has also been enjoying success on TV with the recently released fourth season of Taylor Sheridan's Tulsa King. Now, another Stallone favorite just got an exciting update.

The film in question is a ‘90s cult classic survival thriller with Stallone as a mountain-rescue expert. A plane heist goes wrong, the aircraft blows up, and three suitcases holding $100 million are scattered across the mountains. The criminals then fake a distress call to lure Stallone’s character and his former partner into the wilderness, and force them to use their climbing skills to track down the missing money.

The film is none other than Cliffhanger, which, ironically, doesn’t end on one. It was directed by Renny Harlin, the same filmmaker behind other beloved classics like Deep Blue Sea and Die Hard 2, and it was a huge blockbuster hit when it came out in theaters. The film grossed a whopping $255 million worldwide against a $70 million budget. Now, it is about to gain a whole new life because it has finally landed on Netflix as of November 1.

This newfound attention is going to be great, because the franchise is being rebooted as a feature film slated for 2027. Stallone was initially attached to a direct sequel, but a major creative overhaul in 2024 led to his departure, and he is completely disconnected from this one. With Stallone gone, the reboot needs all the goodwill it can get, and a Netflix debut is a great way to remind longtime fans why they loved the original.

The upcoming reboot will be directed by Jaume Collet-Serra, who has already proven his directing chops with thrillers like Carry-On, House of Wax, and Orphan. Early plot details pitch the reboot as a father-daughter take on Die Hard. It’ll be a kidnapping story where veteran mountaineer Ray Cooper (Pierce Brosnan) is taken hostage on his weekend retreat, and his daughter Naomi (Lily James) has to face her fears and cross the brutal alpine peaks to save her family.

Cliffhanger is available to stream now on Netflix.

‘Resident Evil,’ ‘Primetime’ and more are streaming this week

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After a couple of quiet weeks, November is starting with a packed slate of new movies across the best streaming services. There’s plenty to watch in the coming days, including new arrivals on Netflix, Hulu, Peacock and AMC+. Plus, there are new picks on premium streaming.

Starting with the latter, this week on PVOD you can buy or rent acclaimed movies like “Resident Evil,” “Primetime” and “Bad Apples.” Meanwhile, Netflix debuts its first Christmas movie of the season, and if you're not ready to deck the halls yet, it's also adding an overlooked romantic crime thriller. Alternatively, Hulu has a farcical comedy sequel, and Peacock has a historical action movie starring Andrew Garfield.

These are just some of the most noteworthy new movies on streaming this week. Below, I’ve rounded up the highlights to save you from having to scroll through each platform to find out what’s new this week. And don’t forget to check out our guide to the top new TV shows, too.

Saoirse Ronan stars in this darkly funny thriller that centers on a school teacher pushed to her breaking point by a disruptive pupil. Ronan is the movie’s biggest asset, with the Oscar-nominated actor delivering a strong leading performance. Where the movie stumbles is progressing beyond its initial setup; the middle portion goes through the motions before a finale that takes a big leap in logic. How that swing lands is a matter of personal opinion; it's definitely divisive.

Maria Spencer (Ronan) is a good-natured primary school teacher fighting a daily battle with rebellious student Danny (Eddie Waller). When Danny pushes her too far, she impulsively locks him in her basement. At first, she regrets her rash decision. However, when her other students start flourishing in the classroom with Danny’s negative influence removed, she resolves to keep the troublemaker trapped.

Watch on Prime Video (buy/rent) starting November 3

Director Zach Cregger (“Weapons,” “Barbarian”) delivers the definitive “Resident Evil” movie. The survival horror series has been adapted numerous times. There are the Paul W. S. Anderson movies starring Milla Jovovich, the quickly canceled Netflix series, and several animated efforts, too. None have managed to convey the feeling of playing a Resident Evil video game as well as Cregger’s intense, fast-paced action-horror.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Rising star Austin Abrams plays a courier, tasked with delivering vital medical supplies to a remote hospital in the franchise’s iconic Raccoon City. Once on location, he finds the place overrun with mutated creatures. “Resident Evil” does lean a little too heavily on comedy at times, but this is the blockbuster movie the series has long deserved.

Watch on Prime Video (buy/rent) starting November 3

2026 is the year of Robert Pattinson. Having already starred in “The Drama” and “The Odyssey,” two of the year’s very best, he’s rounding out the year with a role in “Dune Part 3,” but before that, you can enjoy his latest performance in “Primetime.” A dramatic biopic that chronicles the controversial television show “To Catch a Predator.” Pattinson plays host Chris Hansen, and as always, the British actor fully commits to the role.

Directed by Lance Oppenheim, “Primetime” forgoes the conventional biographical movie approach and instead handles Hansen’s obsession with ratings and unearthing the most immoral sexual deviants possible through the lens of a psychological thriller. “Primetime” has a lot to say about both Hansen, the Dateline NBC show, and the millions of viewers who consumed every second with glee. Like it or loathe it, “Primetime” is most definitely a bold biopic.

Watch on Prime Video (buy/rent) starting November 3

Writer/director Bassam Tariq and star Mahershala Ali team up for this action-thriller that, according to the actor, only came together because Marvel’s “Blade” movie fell apart. The duo met when they were both attached to the MCU project, but after multiple delays and production woes, both moved on, and instead teamed up to make “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.” It would seem we got the better movie in the end.

Rated 96% on Rotten Tomatoes, it’s been labeled an “inventive and tonally unique action flick where Mahershala Ali's soulful performance cuts deepest of all.” In the movie, Ali plays a devoutly religious contract killer who is trying to balance his work, faith, and fatherhood. However, when his wife dies, he’s left as the sole carer for three children and must protect them from the consequences of his murderous profession.

Watch on Prime Video (buy/rent) starting November 3

Netflix’s holiday slate starts rolling out this week, and first up is “A Dog’s Perfect Christmas,” a family-focused comedy-drama based on the novel by W. Bruce Cameron, author of “A Dog’s Purpose.” This holiday movie certainly doesn’t look to be doing anything new in the genre, but any flick with an adorable dog at its core is sure to be popular.

It stars Dennis Quaid, Milo Ventimiglia and Jennifer Tilly. Curiously, Quaid actually starred in the movie version of “A Dog’s Purpose,” but this isn’t a sequel. Quaid is playing a new character here.

Netflix’s Christmas crowd-pleaser focuses on the Goss family, whose festive season is thrown into disarray by a medical emergency. With the humans rapidly losing their holiday spirit, it’s up to the family’s wise basset hound, Winstead (voiced by Thomas Haden Church), and a new arrival, an adorable Corgi puppy, to bring the Goss clan back together.

“Super Troopers” fans had to wait 17 years between the first movie and its sequel, so a mere eight-year wait for the trilogy capper, “Super Troopers 3,” probably felt comparatively fast. The cult comedy series from the Broken Lizard crew is a real underdog franchise, and this second sequel is definitely one for the dedicated fans. Its critical reception was lukewarm, but “Super Troopers 3” is sure to delight anybody who’s been watching the antics of this bumbling group of highway patrol troopers since the very start in the early 2000s.

This time there’s love in the air as Farva (Kevin Heffernan) gets engaged to Sarita (Hannah Simone), sister of fellow trooper Thorny (Jay Chandrasekhar). As the wedding approaches, Thorny is desperate to break up the relationship by any means. At the same time, the gang must crack a new drug ring. Expect silly gags and outrageous hijinks.

“Carolina Caroline” is one of 2026’s best movies you (probably) missed in theaters. The crime thriller starring Samara Weaving and Kyle Gallner takes clear inspiration from genre classic “Bonnie and Clyde,” depicting two lovebirds on a criminal spree across the Southern United States. Despite strong reviews, it made little impression at the box office, but could be set to break out now that it’s arriving on Netflix this week.

Looking to escape her small Texas town where she feels unsatisfied with her life, Caroline Daniels (Samara Weaving) impulsively runs away with a charismatic con man (Kyle Gallner), and the two become a notorious criminal duo, engaging in everything from quick hustles to more elaborate heists. As Caroline (Weaving) slips further into the role of a scam artist, she becomes seduced by a world where she can pretend to be anybody she wishes.

“Jason Bourne” director Paul Greengrass’s new historical action movie “The Uprising” found itself at the center of a bizarre marketing campaign over the summer. The movie is based on the 1381 English Peasants' Revolt, which is said to have inspired the stories of Robin Hood. For a brief period, it was claimed “The Uprising” was actually an origin story for the famous (fictional) outlaw, before this was hastily walked back. As for the movie itself, it’s a serviceable historical drama, let down by an ill-conceived ending and a slow middle portion.

In 14th-century England, the ordinary folk are besieged by a plague sweeping Europe and a harsh new tax imposed by King Richard II (Woody Norman) and his inner circle of advisors. Andrew Garfield plays an unnamed rural farmer who leads a full-scale revolt against the established order. Banding together with his fellow commoners, they march on London, with plans to free the young King from the oligarchic influence they believe has led him astray.

“Reacher’s” Alan Ritchson stars in this action-thriller film from director Potsy Ponciroli. On the surface, it looks and sounds like your typical revenge movie. However, there is a wrinkle here that makes “Motor City” a little more interesting. Dialogue is kept to a minimum, with the plot instead driven by a rocking soundtrack and over-the-top action sequences. It’s an experimental approach to storytelling that isn’t wholly successful, but is certainly unique.

Set in 1970s Detroit, John Miller (Ritchson) is a Vietnam veteran and factory worker framed for a crime he didn’t commit by a ruthless gangster named Reynolds (Ben Foster). Adding insult to injury, Reynolds also steals Miller’s girlfriend (Shailene Woodley). After breaking out of prison, Miller embarks on a quest for revenge, and with nothing left to lose, he will stop at nothing until he gets his vengeance.

#3485. My Favorite Travel Headphones Are $250 Off Right Now

As a headphone reviewer, not many headphones outside of the flagship Sony, Bose, and Apple models get me excited. However, the JBL Tour One M3 Smart Tx headphones became the exception to that rule when I started using them over my Sony 1000XM6 as my go-to headphones. And right now, the Tour One M3s are down to $199.95 (originally $449.95), their lowest price ever, according to price-tracking tools. This is a great deal for these headphones, which I deemed my favorite travel headphones in my review.

Everything from design to the features on the Tour One M3 was made with travel in mind. The headphones are very light, which, along with the comfortable soft earcups and headband, makes them great for wearing for long periods of time. I was able to wear these on a long flight without feeling any discomfort. Feeling like you're not wearing any headphones is the gold standard for comfort, and the Tour One M3 nails that aspect. The battery life is also impressive, with up to 70 hours with ANC off and 40 hours with it on.

The travel case is compact, convenient, and has extra storage for the audio transmitter, which is the best feature of the Tour One M3. This is a high-quality, low-latency audio transmitter. The main way most people will use these headphones is by plugging them into the in-flight entertainment, which lets you watch movies in high-quality LDAC with ANC. But I've also been able to use them to watch TV.

The Tour One M3 Smart Tx are incredible traveling headphones, especially at $199.95, and I recommend them to anyone who values comfort, battery life, simplicity, and likes the idea of the audio transmitter.

#3484. iPadOS 27.2: Two new features just upgraded your iPad

iPadOS 27.2 arrived this week as the latest noteworthy iPad software update, here are two new features it includes.

Siri AI is a major improvement over the old Siri, and I’m using it all the time on my iPad—often with a CMD + Space keyboard shortcut since Siri and Spotlight are now integrated.

In iPadOS 27.2, Apple added another convenient way to interact with Siri that first debuted on the Mac in macOS Golden Gate.

When you select text in iPadOS 27.2 via a trackpad or mouse, there’s a new Siri contextual popup that appears to the left of your selection. If you hover over the Siri icon with your cursor, it instantly expands to offer an ‘Ask Siri’ text field.

This makes it quick and easy to ask Siri about whatever you’ve highlighted. And if you’re in the writing process, the Siri popup even has suggestions like ‘Proofread,’ ‘Rewrite,’ and ‘How does this sound?’ so you can get help with just a click.

Siri AI also includes several new upgrades that make it more capable. Per Apple’s release notes:

iPads make great video devices whether you’re an adult or a kid. And if you share an iPad with a partner or child, the Apple TV app has a welcome new addition: user profiles.

iPadOS 27.2 brings over the same profiles feature that tvOS already offered on Apple TV 4K.

When you open the Apple TV app on iPad, you’ll see a new profile selection screen at startup. From here, you can choose who’s watching and the TV app will automatically update its queue, playback history, and content recommendations based on your selection.

If you’re a parent, profiles will take content restrictions into account. So when your child’s profile is active, they’ll only see films and TV shows that match the age settings you’ve previously set.

And if you don’t want to use profiles, it’s easy to disable them from showing on startup with a quick tap.

For more new features available in iPadOS 27.2, see our coverage here.

#3483. Superman's Most Dangerous Villain Unleashes Diabolical New Attack To Break DC's Greatest Hero

Everybody's reasonably come to expect nothing less than absolute benevolence from Kal-El in his most compelling major iteration. Absolute Superman has put its star through the emotional gauntlet, unearthing horrific trafficking, being constantly put up against twisted versions of classic foes who are otherwise peaceful, and on the other end of this is one of his most iconic nemeses, Brainiac. Absolute Brainiac's reign of terror has seen human beings twisted into unrecognizable killing machines, and while he's sent plenty of power to face Kal-El, he mostly wants to break his spirits. Even in their final showdown, this hasn't appeared to let up.

While full pages will surface soon, the preview for Absolute Superman #25 has set up the latest literal salvo of sadism put out by Brainiac, using "an endless supply of indentured clones of himself", he launches his horde head-on against Superman. It seemed as though the miniaturizing of Brainiac's ship was to hide from Superman, but instead, it appears to set up another twisted blow to his resolve, sending countless living clones to knowingly be slaughtered by crashing into Superman mid-flight. It's only the latest in a bold series of swings by this most deranged of Brainiacs from DC's modern era.

Generally speaking, aside from grittier turns for Superman such as in Man of Steel, Absolute Superman has stuck pretty consistently to the hero's no-kill rule. He's actively avoided taking such a direction many times now, with perhaps Toyman's offense being the closest readers have come to seeing Kal-El in an unchecked rage, but he's been able to avoid killing his antagonists as long as possible. While one may quibble about technicalities, Brainiac's clones being flung at him as a sort of countermeasure treated living beings as fodder, with the striking image of them splattering against Superman being no less grim. They may be more drone-like than him by comparison, but that might not be seen by Superman the same way.

As Superman noted, the combination of Brainiac's army of clones and miniaturization technology that are rather common in DC lore with a deeply sadistic "lead" Brainiac makes "a recipe for horror." It's the big showdown everybody's been waiting for, so the key villain of this saga is undoubtedly pulling out his dirtiest tricks ahead of a promised new status quo for Absolute Superman. After all, this final confrontation kicks off Superman's spacefaring quest that'll soon bring him into an encounter with the Phantom Zone. Brainiac, even if soundly defeated either temporarily or permanently in this universe, has had a profound effect on Superman, and has one more chance to leave lasting scars.

Jason Aaron and Rafa Sandoval have successfully crafted a gratifying, emotionally resonant story building up Superman, while breaking him down at just the right moment. There have been magnificently heartbreaking chapters like in issue #14, but much of the recent heartache has been engineered by Brainiac. Atomic Skull's story has been turned into much more of a tragedy, and Christopher Smith's turn as Metallo is so hauntingly dark in just how much the former drone-turned-mastermind broke his mind and altered his body. Perhaps most dark of all is Brainiac's massacre of Lex Luthor's family, which up to this point had yet to produce any meaningful results other than inducing enough trauma to, in his eyes, hopefully awaken the iconic Earthling menace.

Superman's most brilliant long-running adversary is moving up not just in power levels, but dark ambitions for the multiverse and all known futures.

The more people he's thrown in Superman's way, the more Absolute Brainiac has tested his enemy's resolve in inventive and unforgivable ways. Brainiac appears to have even pushed Superman past thresholds he never planned on crossing, like killing in this latest issue, and subjected him to immense psychological torture. He's already become an unforgettable menace, and even if he fails to awaken the villainous ego possibly dormant in Luthor, he still took the most extreme, brutal method to massacre an innocent family Superman could not save. Such a trail of blood and misery is hard to look past, even as the story moves on from this point soon.

#3482. You Can Get These 'Nothing' Over-Ear Headphones for $55 Right Now

Nothing, the upstart U.K. brand that makes products like phones, smartwatches, and headphones, has quickly become one of my favorite players in tech. Its products offer unique features and designs, and the prices are competitive. For example, right now, Nothing's latest budget over-ear headphones, which were released in October 2025, the CMF Headphone Pros, are just $55 (originally $99). This is a great option for anyone looking to get reasonably priced over-the-ear headphones that punch above their weight when it comes to performance.

Much like Nothing's CMF Buds Pro 2 earbuds, the CMF Headphone Pros are budget headphones that don't feel like it. They're an affordable alternative to the popular Headphone 1 (currently $199), and seamlessly integrate into the Nothing/CMF ecosystem, which includes smartphones, watches, and other audio products. There is a companion Nothing X app that allows you to customize action buttons, among other things, but the cool thing about these headphones is the control you get without needing the app.

There is a multi-function roller on one side of the headphone that you can roll to adjust volume or press to control the ANC modes, which include adaptive ANC (adjusting cancellation/transparency in real-time) and Spatial Audio (creates an immersive, 3D soundstage for music/movies). On the other side, you'll find an "Energy Slider," which tunes your sound in real-time, instantly adjusting the treble and bass balance.

You'll get an impressive 100 hours of playback on a single charge (reduced to up to 50 hours with ANC turned on) as well as AAC, SBC, and LDAC support. They have an IPX2 rating for resistance against sweat, and there is a 3.5mm audio jack for wired listening.

Nothing is known for its minimalistic design, but these headphones do a bit more by allowing you to mix and match the earcups with different colors (sold separately for $25). These are a good option for those looking for stylish, budget over-ear headphones that have great battery life and excellent audio quality for their price point.

#3481. iOS 27.2 adds new Find My feature at just the right time

iOS 27.2 is here, and alongside new features for Apple Photos, Messages, and Siri AI, the update also has a welcome addition for Find My: support for Apple TV 4K remotes.

Find My has long been the iPhone’s go-to hub for locating people as well as your Apple devices.

Except until now, there’s been one Apple device not included in the app.

The Siri Remote for Apple TV 4K has historically been absent from Find My. There was another way to locate it using the Remote app via Control Center, but most users probably didn’t realize that feature existed.

But with iOS 27.2, Apple TV remotes have now been added to the Find My app for location tracking. Open Find My in iOS 27.2 and go to the Devices tab, and compatible Siri Remotes (2nd gen and later) will now appear there.

It’s nice that Apple finally addressed this oversight, but the timing is no coincidence. That’s because the new Siri Remote (4th gen) is going to make finding a lost remote way easier.

That's great but I just discovered that my Apple Watch series 10 does not have the ability to notify me if I leave my iPhone behind. I can use Find My to see where the phone is, but it doesn't give me a notification alert. My series 7 watch had that ability and I'm shocked that the series 10 does not. This was confirmed to me by an Apple tech support technician this morning.

The new remote features Precision Finding support and a built-in speaker. So the next time it’s lost somewhere in your house, your iPhone can direct you step-by-step to its location and trigger a noise to help.

The new Siri Remote is included with the 4th generation Apple TV 4K. But you can also buy it separately for $59 and get the same new features.

The upgraded remote is compatible with all Apple TV 4K and Apple TV HD models. To benefit from Precision Finding though, you’ll need an iPhone 17 or newer.

Did you know the Remote app offered support for finding a lost remote? Will you use the new feature in Find My? Let us know in the comments.

#3480. The 10 Most Elite Movies of 2026 So Far, Ranked

Each year, doomsayers are ready to pronounce cinema dead. Since the pandemic, 2026 has been the most triumphant and encouraging year for the medium, particularly regarding theatrical exhibition, with a handful of unexpected hits dominating the zeitgeist. This year has proven that you don't need a giant superhero epic to draw people to theaters, as everything from romantic horror movies to A24 documentaries have brought casual audiences to their local multiplex. 2026 has seen many of the highest-grossing movies of all time and a collection of gems and soon-to-be classics, including this list of the ten best of the year so far, ranked.

In a year filled with unexpected plot twists and revelations, The Drama took the cake as the most shocking cinematic confession of the year. The Drama, a hilariously macabre and provocative black comedy-drama by Kristoffer Borgli, was the first of three collaborations by Zendaya and Robert Pattinson, and their most dynamic on-screen partnership. The film touched third rails, but it wasn't edgy for the sole purpose of shock value.

On the precipice of their wedding, Emma Harwood (Zendaya) discloses a horrifying and unsettling secret from her youth, which causes her fiancé, Charlie Thompson (Pattinson), to spiral, reckoning with his decision to devote his life to this woman. A film that's often hard to watch due to its cringe-inducing social faux pas and uncomfortable confrontations with society's most taboo subjects, The Drama is nonetheless fascinated by the politics of romantic relationships, as well as the conflicts that arise when people give themselves over to each other. There's a real heart to the romance between Emma and Charlie that balances out Borgli's pitch-black humor and dissection of American values. The Norwegian filmmaker asks: are Americans too prude or too crass? Either way, the combination is destructive.

A movie that's slipped through the cracks during the busy fall lineup, Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is the film that should keep Disney up at night. After failing to get their Blade movie off the ground as part of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, director Bassam Tariq and star Mahershala Ali finally dropped out and teamed up to make Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, a bold action-thriller that's both rip-roaring and thoughtful as a reflection of Muslim identity.

Lesson learned for Hollywood: don't overthink the project and give Tariq and Ali enough resources to make a crowd-pleasing and socially conscious film, and you should expect greatness. The film was a glorious return for the two-time Oscar winner of Moonlight and Green Book, who gives perhaps his signature movie-star turn as Latif, an ex-military hitman who carries out jobs for a religious leader caught in the crossfire of Islamic and Christian forces while raising his kids as a single dad. Your Mother's fight choreography is as good, if not superior, to, anything you'll see in a major blockbuster, and its combat is a fresh evolution after years of John Wick clones. Tariq tells a deeply personal and urgent story of a conflicted assassin who struggles with his faith.

Trust us, accept Oliva Wilde's invitation to this raunchy, scintillating, and candid dramedy about all the things most people aren't ready to talk about. The Invite, a single-location, adult-oriented character study about two couples discussing sex, career ambition, and familial responsibility versus individualism, is the kind of movie that used to release regularly from the studio system. Now that they are a rare breed in 2026, films like The Invite feel like a festive celebration, but maybe not as freaky as whatever is going on in this film's apartment.

When an on-the-rocks, tense married couple, Angela (Wilde) and Joe (Seth Rogen), invite their enigmatic upstairs neighbors, the quirky and feisty couple, Pina (Penélope Cruz) and Hawk (Edward Norton), they reconsider their entire lives and the status of their relationship, as truths unspool and hard feelings are laid out on the table during this wild dinner party. A stylish hybrid between a raunchy comedy and an intimate chamber drama, The Invite appeals to a wide audience, even with its commentary that's designed to reflect on your own discomfort. Wilde's precise behind-the-camera vision gives the film the edge of a psychological thriller, as the canted angles and intricate blocking create an uncanny vibe and awkward tension, a sentiment that everyone who's ever been paired up with an odd couple can relate to.

2026's first tentpole release, Project Hail Mary continues to linger in film culture since its release in March. Based on an Andy Weir novel and directed by Phil Lord and Chris Miller after a 12-year hiatus from the director's chair, the film was an inspired box office smash hit, as it offered a glimmer of hope for audiences that star-driven, non-franchise event movies can still thrive. The year was a big winner for Ryan Gosling and hand-crafted, practical effects.

A charismatic screen icon, a rock puppet, and an outer-space journey about going home and teamwork. What more else could you ask for? Project Hail Mary reinvigorated the traditional four-quadrant blockbuster after years of studios neglecting so many of its creative principles. The film, despite its PG-13 rating, is something that people of ostensibly all ages can enjoy, and its melancholic streak and sci-fi wizardry keep the cinephiles in the theater locked in. Dr. Ryland Grace (Gosling) is the idyllic movie protagonist—amiable, courageous, and sometimes naive. It is the part of a lifetime for Gosling, who has become a master of bumbling humor and dramatic sincerity, and Lord and Miller let their pop culture obsessions soar to the moon.

This is certainly a controversial pick, to put it mildly. Even when accepting some of the writing shortcomings and plot dynamics, Disclosure Day is yet another awe-inspiring, luminous vision by the legendary Steven Spielberg. One of 2026's most divisive movies left a bad taste in some viewers' mouths, but for those who were on its wavelength, the film's majestic scope and hyper-earnest tone made this feel like the most important cinematic statement of the year.

Featuring a career-best performance by Emily Blunt and Spielberg operating behind the camera as if he hasn't aged, time will be kind to this misunderstood achievement.

Disclosure Day, which saw Spielberg returning to the alien subgenre, is a mega-sized blockbuster/auteurist expression of many layers. A conspiracy thriller, sci-fi mystery, and existential drama wrapped into one, the film was criticized for being a retrograde and out-of-touch depiction of contemporary America and our relationship to government secrets coming from a septuagenarian filmmaker, but Spielberg's optimism is magnificently used to wrestle with contemporary cynicism. Disclosure Day posits a world where people's skepticism and ulterior motives shatter in the face of something truly profound. The film, filled with intense chase sequences and moving character moments, is far stranger and thematically inscrutable than Spielberg's usual fare. Featuring a career-best performance by Emily Blunt and Spielberg operating behind the camera as if he hasn't aged, time will be kind to this misunderstood achievement.

Why don't you have a seat over there? Primetime, starring Robert Pattinson (arguably the MVP of 2026) as To Catch a Predator's Chris Hansen, is an essential watch and one of the most striking films of the year. The first narrative feature by documentarian Lance Oppenheim, this surrealistic, unconventional biopic about one of the 2000s most polarizing media figures is a dazzling and off-putting morality fable about the sinister nature of performance art and vigilante justice.

Now 20 years removed from the height of To Catch a Predator's popularity on NBC, Primetime reflects on this bizarre and unruly era for culture from a contemporary lens. Oppenheim dives into this period by mimicking the visual and tonal style of an America obsessed with trashy reality TV, resulting in a hypnotic aesthetic that pushes the medium to new realms. Even if he has the moral high ground relative to the sexual predators that the show is incriminating, it takes a warped mind to make a living off turning federal prosecutions into performance art for millions at home on a Thursday night. Primetime, carried by Pattinson in the performance of the year, captures the world through Hansen's obsessions and unseemly desires. The film speaks to present-day perils by depicting an America where our heroes are on television, glorifying the hunt for sex offenders as a circus act, and where the media is our only outlet for justice.

One of the many movies of 2026 that needed to be seen to be believed, Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie is unlike anything audiences have ever seen on the big screen. Explaining Matt Johnson's style and the premise of the Canadian web series that the film is based on, which has no affiliation with the famous grunge band, is a tall task, but anyone with a good sense of humor and fervent passion for creative companionship will adore all the madness that's under the hood of this time-traveling music mockumentary.

For Matt Johnson and series co-creator Jay McCarrol, playing themselves in the film, the goal is to land a gig at the Rivoli nightclub in Toronto, but when inadvertently traveling back in time to 2008, they stumble into a chance to attain fame that will carry them to the present day. Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie's audacious concept doesn't disappoint in the final product, as Johnson and McCarrol put on the most electric, hilarious, and sweeping adventure that satirizes showbiz, movie history, and culture, best exemplified in the initial arrival in 2008, before the fall from grace of various canceled celebrities and societal rejections of insensitive humor. With the right crowd, Nirvanna the Band plays like a rock concert, with every joke and suspenseful, jaw-dropping set piece leaving the room completely enraptured.

Many inventive and groundbreaking movies entered the cultural zeitgeist in 2026, but there are still a handful of smaller, arthouse films that likely slipped past your radar. Look no further than Blue Heron, another crowning achievement of Canadian cinema and the announcement of a new visionary, Sophy Romvari. This personal, gut-wrenching, and transcendent portrait of grief and the erosion of memory is sure to leave you speechless and exploring your own soul.

The meaning of life, family, and distant memories are beautifully reflected in Romvari's debut feature film, which follows a filmmaker, Sasha (Eylul Guven as a child and Amy Zimmer as an adult), recalling a summer in the '90s when her brother's disruptive behavior, the result of untreated mental illness, caused a strain in her household in Vancouver. As a family drama, Blue Heron is palpably sensitive, sparking an array of Proustian memories where the minuscule incidents trigger the most harrowing sensations. The film's somber register evokes Romvari and her avatar trying to repress emotions, as the director is still trying to grasp why these memories continue to linger. This meta-textual, deconstructionist story about the stories we tell ourselves to make sense of the past shifts into gear in its second half, where the audience wrestles with how we treat male mental illness and the mind's constant longing to rewrite history.

In terms of scope, anticipation, critical discussion, and cultural omnipresence, The Odyssey will undoubtedly stand as the cinematic event of the year, if not the decade. Christopher Nolan, with yet another critically acclaimed, auteurist blockbuster under his belt, proved himself to be the most viable name in Hollywood, more than any other living movie star. His biggest swing yet gave you everything you wanted out of a major motion picture extravaganza ripe with humanity, grace, and pathos.

Rounded out by an absurdly stacked cast, including Matt Damon as Odysseus, Tom Holland as Telemachus, and Anne Hathaway as Penelope, The Odyssey was something everyone had to be part of in some way. Each star, even the surprise scene-stealers like Samantha Morton and Elliot Page, helped craft the modern-day classical epic. Nolan, who miraculously shot the entire movie on IMAX film, painted with his broadest canvas yet, but he never lost his control, momentum, and probing psychology that have made him the signature visionary of his generation. A stunningly intimate epic about trauma, destiny, and legacy, The Odyssey grounded the overwhelming scale of Homer's epic poem without minimizing the all-encompassing weight of the text. Nolan, who brought a fresh take on an ancient story, is perhaps the quintessential storyteller of our modern world.

Rarely do you see a feature film garner this much online buzz and sheer curiosity, let alone a documentary. However, anyone with an ounce of awareness of Nathan Fielder knew that You Can See Everything, a film we didn't even know existed two months ago, would break the confines of the documentary form. Chronicling convicted Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes before she's sent to prison and much more, the film, co-directed by Lance Oppenheim, showed the glowing potential for cinema in the 2020s as a form-breaking artistic expression about everything and nothing at the same time, which is what living in the present day feels like.

No logline does You Can See Everything justice, as Fielder and Oppenheim's cinéma vérité coverage of Holmes and her partner Billy Evans evolves into a bizarre, unsettling, and hypnotic dissection of filmmaking, egoism, performance art, and parasocial relationships. For avid fans of Nathan for You and The Rehearsal, the shocking box office hit and potential awards player upends the Fielder we've grown to love or despise, as his deadpan awkwardness shatters in the face of the curious case of Elizabeth Holmes, who develops an uncanny relationship with her documentarian as Fielder attempts to read and connect with her. The film, which features a second-half shift in perspective that's becoming harder and harder to keep from being spoiled, reflects how some people are born incapable of truth and basic communication. You Can See Everything is the cultural text of the year, as its depiction of morally grey tech moguls and constant nonfiction image-making taps directly into our hearts.

#3479. Seven Of Nine Officially Goes Full Borg In Star Trek: Federation Fleet

Arguably no other Star Trek character has endured a more tumultuous journey than Seven of Nine, whose struggle to reclaim her humanity after years of assimilation became one of the defining storylines of Star Trek: Voyager. Originally known as Annika Hansen, Seven was assimilated by the Borg as a child, losing her individuality and becoming another drone in the Collective.

Although Captain Janeway and Voyager's crew eventually liberated her, escaping the Borg's control was only the beginning of her journey. Over the years, Seven has repeatedly struggled with her Borg roots, even temporarily reconnecting with the Collective during the events of Star Trek: Picard. Despite eventually becoming a Starfleet captain, her past has never stopped shaping the person she is today, for better or worse.

Now, as Star Trek prepares for another exciting release, Seven's complicated relationship with the Borg is taking a dark turn, with a surprising new appearance that longtime fans won't want to miss.

Seven of Nine is officially going full Borg again, thanks to an exciting new release arriving on November 13. As part of Magic: The Gathering's massive Star Trek crossover, the beloved Voyager character is receiving a new card that revisits her original identity within the Collective. Interestingly, "Seven of Nine, Tertiary Adjunct" will be featured in two separate Commander decks: Federation Fleet and We Are the Borg.

The "Seven of Nine, Tertiary Adjunct" card, illustrated by Bastien L. Deharme, depicts Seven in her Borg form, complete with the mechanical enhancements associated with her time as a drone. She's classified as a Legendary Artifact Creature — Borg, with 1/4 power and toughness and an ability called "That Is Irrelevant." Players can tap Seven to draw a card and then discard one, placing two charge counters on an artifact if the discarded card isn't a land.

Perhaps the most interesting detail, however, is the card's flavor text, which features one of Seven's most memorable lines:

Longtime fans will recognize this as Seven's very first spoken line in Star Trek: Voyager, specifically Season 4, Episode 1, "Scorpion, Part II," which originally aired on September 3, 1997. During the episode, Captain Janeway negotiates an uneasy alliance with the Borg to fight Species 8472, demanding a representative that can directly communicate with her crew. Seven emerges as the Collective's spokesperson, introducing herself by her full Borg designation.

Of course, Seven eventually escapes the Collective and begins rediscovering her humanity, making her appearance in both Commander decks fitting. Federation Fleet is led by Jean-Luc Picard, with Captain Janeway serving as its alternative commander. Meanwhile, We Are the Borg is led by the Borg Queen, with Locutus of Borg as another commander option. Seven is effectively playable on both sides of the Federation's longstanding conflict with the Borg, which makes perfect sense given her complicated history.

The larger Magic: The Gathering x Star Trek crossover officially launches on November 13, 2026, celebrating the franchise's 60th anniversary. Alongside Federation Fleet and We Are the Borg, fans can pick up Landing Party, led by Spock, and Klingon Fury, led by Worf.

Each Commander deck includes 100 cards, including 32 new-to-Magic cards, with premium Collector's Editions featuring surge foil treatments throughout. The crossover also includes a larger collection of cards celebrating characters, starships, and memorable moments from across Star Trek's history.

For Seven of Nine fans, the new card offers a nostalgic look back to the character's earliest days in Star Trek, long before she became one of Starfleet's most unlikely captains.

Here’s the spine-friendly exercise you should be doing

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I suffer from sciatica, so I have to be mindful when it comes to ab exercises like crunches and sit-ups, which typically put a lot of stress on the lower back. In the run-up to my last marathon, I asked my physical therapist for an ab exercise that would build core strength and stability without stressing my back — read on to find out what he said next.

As a reminder, what works for me might not work for you or your body. If you’re a complete beginner, pregnant or postpartum, or recovering from an injury or surgery, it’s always best to seek personalized advice from a qualified professional.

When it comes to a spine-safe way to work your core, the main exercise my therapist recommended is the bird-dog. Read on to find out how to do a bird dog with perfect form, its benefits, plus two other back-friendly exercises to add to your routine.

Unlike crunches, which force your back to bend as you lift your head, neck, and shoulders off the mat, bird dog teaches your abdominal muscles to hold your spine in place while your limbs move. This helps build the functional fitness you need for everyday life, as well as during sports like running.

As you perform the bird dog, you’ll be working the deep stabilizer muscles that run along the spine and glutes, rather than the outer six-pack muscles. The deep core works as the body’s corset and helps protect your spine from injury.

Here’s how to do the bird dog exercise with good form:

Another safe exercise to try if you suffer from lower back pain is the dead bug. Again, unlike a crunch or a plank, this exercise targets those all-important deep abdominal muscles while keeping your lower back supported.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

A huge benefit of the dead bug is that it’s performed lying flat on your back, meaning there is no compressive load on your spinal discs, as you’re not having to fight gravity to hold the pose. This allows you to build core strength and train yourself to maintain a neutral spine without triggering any pain in your lower back.

If this is too much for you, start with bent-knee taps. Instead of straightening your leg, keep your knee bent and tap one heel down to the floor, then bring it back to your starting position and repeat on the other side.

For the final move in this spine-safe series, the glute bridge is a great exercise for strengthening the glutes, hamstrings, and lower back stabilizers without putting pressure on your spine.

The core isn’t just the muscles that sit on the front of your body — it also includes the erector spinae (the muscles running along your spine) and the multifidus (the deep stabilizing muscles in the lower back). This exercise works these muscles, as well as waking up sleepy glutes. If your glutes don’t fire properly, your lower back muscles can overcompensate, leading to tight back muscles.

#3475. ‘VisionQuest’s T’Nia Miller Breaks Down Jocasta’s “Godlike, Badass” Moment in Episode 7

Taylor Gates is an Indiana native who earned her BFA in Creative Writing from the University of Evansville. She fell in love with entertainment by watching shows about chaotic families like Full House, The Nanny, Gilmore Girls, and The Fosters. After college, she moved to Los Angeles to pursue a career as a writer, editor, and filmmaker. Today, she’s a sucker for dramedies — especially coming-of-age stories centering around complex female and LGBTQ+ characters. She has been with Collider since May 2022.

Editor's Note: The following contains spoilers for VisionQuest Episode 7.

T’Nia Miller is a true powerhouse performer. Her range is incredible, spanning everything from intense horror and devastating drama to trippy sci-fi and political thriller. She has a long list of impressive credits, including Mike Flanagan series The Haunting of Bly Manor and The Fall of the House of Usher; Russell T. Davies shows Years and Years, Banana, and Cucumber; Apple TV’s Foundation; and Sex Education.

Her newest role is Jocasta in Marvel’s VisionQuest. Mysterious, ambitious, and endlessly fascinating, we are first introduced to Jocasta as the Butcherbird Killer before finding out that she’s actually an AI version of the brilliant scientist Josephine Carrington. She’s hellbent on controlling humanity, and yet, Miller doesn’t play her as a straightforward evil villain by any means. She’s highly complicated and morally grey, which really comes out during her spicy and twisted but also surprisingly moving scenes with Ultron (James Spader).

Collider got the chance to speak to Miller about her work on the series. During the conversation, she broke down Ultron and Jocasta’s complex, irresistible dynamic, all those references to motherhood and Edgar Allan Poe, those major reveals in Episode 7, and more.

COLLIDER: I absolutely love your character and performance. You're kind of playing multiple roles in one, between Butcherbird Killer, AI Jocasta, and human scientist Josephine Carrington. How did you approach bringing all of these identities together into this one character?

T’NIA MILLER: Well, I think she is just one identity. I think we're multifaceted — I think we're all of those people. Although Jo Carrington isn't a genocidal maniac, mass murderer, serial killer, I do believe that, at the core of Jocasta, she is Jo Carrington, right? So it all stems from that place. And then the other things are just circumstantial, as it were. It's just like, “Which hat am I wearing today?” I'm sure a different side of Taylor shows up when you're with your friends, when we're with your mom, when you're at work, so that's how I see it.

That’s so interesting. I think you're right — you peel back all of these layers of her. I absolutely love her dynamic with Ultron because it's so twisted and sexy, but also kind of pure and sweet at the same time. Were there any specific conversations or exercises you did with James to build that dynamic that's so unique and also authentic at the same time?

MILLER: The first time I met James was on set.

MILLER: Yeah, we were about to shoot a scene, but we were shooting chronologically. So that first meeting was in Episode 5, and we were sitting with [director] Vincenzo Natali. I love working with Vincenzo. I’ve worked with him before, so I instantly felt comfortable. It is a cat-and-mouse game. It's like, “I'm going to seduce and flirt with you” because it’s her language. “You have something that’s mine, so I’m going to get it.” And James is doing Ultron in that space. The writing is there, so you're doing what's on the page. It also happened to be my audition piece for Jocasta, so I sort of felt like I knew it. That was my intro into her world, and we just built it from there. And as the series went along, so did their relationship — Jocasta and Ultron’s — as did James and my relationship, and understanding, and care.

I remember there was one night where I couldn't remember my lines, and I was just having a moment. We were in Madripoor. It was tiny — it was, like, four lines or something — and he says, “I think he’d hold you. Is it okay if I hold you for this scene? I'll just hold you to support you. I said, “Thank you. I apologize. I’m so sorry.” He said, “You never have to apologize to me.” He held my arm, and I know that, at that moment, that was James.

That's so sweet. I love that. You can really feel the chemistry on screen. One of my favorite scenes in the show is the beginning of Episode 6 where Jo is like, “This is chess, except they're my pieces, my board, and I'm the queen.”

MILLER: I wanted to swear on that! I wanted to say, “I'm the MFB.”

We'll know in our hearts that she was supposed to say that! Can you talk about that line and that scene in general? There’s so much going on under the surface. It really is a chess game.

MILLER: It is chess. These are their tactics. They're just deploying whatever skills they have, and hers is, “Well, you obviously like me, so I'm going to lean into that.” Then that explodes in her face, but that was a lot of fun — the twists and turns and, at any given moment, who has the upper hand. Those peaks and troughs are so wonderful as an actor — it’s the really good stuff to play.

I noticed the language that's used to describe Jocosta is so maternal. She's called the mother of artificial intelligence, and she refers to the nanos as her children. I'm curious how that language impacted your understanding of her because I thought that was a really interesting choice.

MILLER: It really impacted it, actually. Because for me, I was going to rescue my children. She’s like, “I like you, and I'm attracted to you, but you are not gonna get in the way. You can't distract me from saving my children.” And I am a mother, so I was able to pull from those experiences of fighting for your kids. You have to. I've had to fight for my kids at times in their lives, so that really informed how, no matter what distraction there was, I had to keep my objective firm and clear until those later scenes. I’m like, “Okay, what is my objective? Why am I doing this? What is that about?” And she starts to crumble and question herself, and she begins to understand herself and what has happened to her, which is ultimately sad, and the scars of that trauma.

Four villains, and four arguments the films were honest enough to actually let them make. Here is the one you lean towards, the part of it that holds up, and the exact point where it stops holding up.

You align with the one who was right about the problem and wrong about the solution. Killmonger is the most persuasive villain Marvel has produced because the film never pretends his anger came from nowhere.

You align with the protector, which is the most understandable and most dangerous position on this list. Namor is not chasing power or revenge, he is doing whatever keeps his people hidden, and he has been doing it for centuries.

You align with the patient one, the only man on this list with no powers, no army and no hurry. Zemo lost his family in Sokovia and then spent years working out that you do not fight the Avengers, you introduce them to each other's secrets.

You align with the one who decided the answer was arithmetic. Thanos is not angry and not grieving in any way he will admit to, he simply reached a conclusion and never once revisited it, which is precisely what makes him frightening.

I thought it was also so interesting that there are all these references to “The Raven” and Edgar Allan Poe. I’m curious what you think her ties to that theme say about her, too.

MILLER: She looks to nature for her answers. It's not my first venture with Edgar Allan Poe because I did The Fall of the House of Usher. I was like, “Oh, this is great that it's showing up again.” It’s so funny because I kept seeing starlings all around me during that. I always see these starlings. There's so much to be taken from Poe and his view of the world, and I think that Josephine Carrington and Poe potentially have the same outlook in some ways on our humanity, or lack thereof, and where we should be heading. It’s a tale as old as time.

I love that you mentioned Fall the House of Usher. That and Bly Manor are where I first became familiar with your work. I'm curious if you had any conversations with Terry about your experience with that material or if it was a complete coincidence.

MILLER: I think it was a complete coincidence. Terry's got a million thoughts in his brain at once, and of course, there's a writers’ room.

Episode 7 sees the client wanting to restore Jo’s memories, which is a concept that really scares her. She says she's not really sure she's ready to be her again. Why do you think that fear runs so deeply in her?

MILLER: I think it's a fear that runs through all of us. It's a fear of the unknown. If I may, as humans, we feel like we have some element of control and that we know something, and actually, we know nothing, and we control nothing. I think that's just an echo of that. Why doesn't she want to know? Because that's a person. How did she get in this mess in the first place? Did she have a hand in it? Is it her fault? Who is she gonna have to face? Do I have to face my shadow self? Like, that's scary. What if I was wrong? What have I done? What's that going to unmask? I think she's genuinely petrified of what that means and where that may lead because she's unstable. She says, “I've got all these memories, and I don't know why I feel this anger, and I don't know where it comes from.” That's a trauma for so many women, especially as they get older — it starts to creep up on you. I've got this anger — this displaced anger — and I don't know where it comes from. You know you have to go back and do the work, don't you? I think that's it. I’m sorry to get all philosophical.

No, that's so beautifully said, and I think that's so true! It stands in such an interesting contrast to that moment in Episode 6 where Ultron insists that he wants to know her, even though it'll be painful. What do you think his desire to deeply understand her means to her?

MILLER: Here’s a really terrible analogy: It's like you're faced with a mountain of dishes, and someone says, “You wash, I'll dry.” [Laughs] It’s like, “Okay, I feel supported now. That's a surprise. Do I have a companion in you? Can I trust you?” I think, for her, it's everything — to be able to share it, to be able to be understood.

We get a flashback at the end of Episode 7 where it’s revealed that Josephine won the Stark Award with her partner, and the two of them vowed to be loving gods. I'm curious what that choice of words sort of tells you about her.

MILLER: Well, I think he says gods, and she says, “Yeah, but we'll be loving gods.” There’s a little bit of ego. They've managed to do this thing, and they're gonna save humanity. They're gonna save the world. She couldn't save her father, but she's gonna save everybody else from going through that pain and then some. That's kind of a godlike, badass thing to do, right?

I really hope that we get to see more of her in the MCU. Are there any characters you would like to see her interact with, in particular?

MILLER: Well, [everyone from] Black Panther. I've worked with Letitia Wright twice before, so let’s make it three. We did a play that was written by Danai Gurira, who is also in Black Panther, bizarrely and oddly enough. It was fringe theater earning pennies years and years ago. And then we did a queer show, Cucumber and Banana, with Russell T. Davies. That would be just interesting because it’s a small universe. I think Loki. Wanda.

MILLER: More of Ultron, please and thank you. I'm going to broadly say the Avengers. I'll just go on forever and ever and ever.

These are amazing. I'm wanting a Jennifer Kale moment. She has this potion background, so she’s in STEM, too. I think it could be really fun.

MILLER: Oh my god, that would be cool. That would be very, very, very cool. I see that.

You get to do so many cool action scenes in this show. You're kicking ass, to put it bluntly. What was stuntwork on this like for you? What was the training process?

MILLER: Very early on, I had a few rehearsals, and then I looked at Chloe Kibble, who is my stunt double, and I went, “Okay, Chloe — you're up. You are much better at it than I am.”

MILLER: In The Peripheral and Bly Manor, I got to do some of my own stunts — or part of them — and that was cool. Paul does a lot of his, but this was very, very much Chloe Kibble, who was brilliant and is brilliant. Shoutout to Chloe. I can do a few punches and kicks and stuff, but not the whole fight scene.

DJI may be best known for its drones and camera equipment, but the company has also been expanding into portable power, with the Power 2000 being its most capable standalone power station yet. Essentially a large rechargeable battery, it's designed to provide electricity wherever you might need it, whether that's on a camping trip, at a job site, during an outdoor movie night, or at home when the power goes out. And if you've been considering one for any of those situations, the Power 2000 is currently down to $749.99 from its original $1,299 price, taking nearly $550 off what would otherwise be a fairly expensive investment.

It's about the size of a carry-on suitcase and weighs close to 50 pounds, so it's not something you'd strap to your back, but it fits easily in a car trunk. The battery itself is built to last, rated for 4,000 charges before it starts losing any noticeable capacity. Performance-wise, DJI says the 2,048Wh capacity can keep a refrigerator running for up to 40 hours during a home power outage, charge a laptop 18 times, or power a projector for 18 hours. Those numbers line up with what you’d expect from a unit this size, and they make it useful for both emergencies and planned outdoor use.

You also get a solid mix of ports—there are three AC outlets, a 30-amp port for heavier appliances or RV setups, multiple USB-C ports (including a 140W option for laptops), and DJI’s own SDC ports for direct drone charging. If you use DJI gear, that alone makes life easier in the field, notes this Mashable review. Recharging is also fast for a battery this size. Plugged into a wall outlet, it can go from empty to full in about 90 minutes. You can also top it up with solar panels or from your car, which makes it workable for longer trips. Rounding out its features is its companion app, which lets you check its battery level from your phone without having to walk over to it, a small thing that turns out to be pretty convenient. Note that this unit has no built-in light, which is something many competing power stations include.

We're pretty much done for major phone launches in 2026, certainly for devices that will be coming to the U.S. and Europe, which means it's time to start looking forward to what might be coming next year. And, as usual, we expect the first big release of the year to be Samsung's Galaxy S27 series.

The S27 series is said to be made up of four phones: The Galaxy S27, Galaxy S27 Plus, Galaxy S27 Ultra and the new Galaxy S27 Pro. We've started hearing some rumors about what those phones could have to offer, including one of the first major redesigns Galaxy phones have had for several years. Obviously there are a few things we also really want to see on these phones as well.

So here are the top seven changes we want to see on the Samsung Galaxy S27.

Galaxy battery capacity does not change much, if ever. In fact the Galaxy S Ultra batteries have been stuck on the 5,000 mAh plateau since 2020. Meanwhile companies like OnePlus have been offering over 7,000 mAh batteries without any meaningful change to the design.

Frankly, people are sick of it, and it's time the Galaxy S27 changed that. Thankfully Samsung has shown that it can do this, thanks to the introduction of silicon carbon batteries in the Galaxy Z Fold 8 series. This technology allows for greater energy density, meaning you can offer more battery capacity without increasing the size of the battery.

Rumors suggest this may be happening too, with the S27 Ultra reportedly getting a 5,700 mAh battery. The S27 Pro is tipped to get a 5,200 mAh battery, though we don't know what the S27 and S27 Plus might be getting. We hope they'll get an increase from the 4,300 mAh and 4,900mAh batteries on their S26 counterparts.

One of my biggest gripes with Android phones is how so few of them have adopted the full Qi2 wireless charging standard — complete with the magnetic charging ring. Samsung is one such offender, adding Qi2 charging technology, while relying on special cases to add the magnetic support.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Many reasons have been given over the past couple of years, ranging from issues with the S Pen to the fact the camera bump blocks where the magnetic ring should sit. Whatever the reason, it's high time that Samsung got its act together and added Qi2 magnets to its phones, and the S27 series' redesign is the perfect place to do it.

Brighter screens offer huge visibility benefits, especially in bright conditions, and that shouldn't be affected by a new screen feature. Especially if you're not actually using it.

Samsung has a habit of neglecting the camera hardware on some of its phones, particularly the cheaper models like the Galaxy S26 and Galaxy S26 Plus. 50MP main lenses are fine, but 12MP ultrawide and 10MP telephoto lenses aren't befitting a flagship device. It doesn't matter that they don't bear the Ultra branding.

At the very least the S27 and S27 Plus need a higher resolution ultrawide lens, ideally something closer to 50MP. Any extra upgrades on the telephoto lens will be a nice bonus.

As for the Galaxy S27 Ultra, it's about time we started seeing more advanced camera features. Variable zoom has been rumored for at least a couple of years, and the rumored loss of the secondary telephoto lens feels like the perfect time to offer that. Likewise, now that the iPhone 18 Pro has a variable aperture lens, it's time Samsung brought that particular feature back to its own phones.

Samsung has not been the best at improving charging speed, though it earned some goodwill by upping the Galaxy S26 Ultra's charging speed from 45W to 60W. But sadly the S26 and S26 Plus were left at their old speeds of 25W and 45W, respectively. It's high time that changed.

There's little reason to keep both phones charging so slowly, especially since the Plus and Ultra models shared the same 45W charging speeds for a few years. It's also worth pointing out that the S26 Ultra can wirelessly charge at 25W speeds, which means the standard model really should be running faster by now.

Hopefully the Galaxy S27 series will fix that particular issue, even if the Ultra model sticks at 60W for a little while longer.

I have my concerns about the prospect of a Galaxy S27 Pro, because I'm not entirely sure there's room for another Galaxy flagship to sit between the S27 Plus and S27 Ultra. Certainly not if the other three devices in the lineup are sticking around in their current forms.

What I hope is that Samsung can find some kind of niche for the S27 Pro to ensure that it's not a complete waste of time and money. Ideally without compromising features on the S27 Plus or hiking up the price of the S27 Ultra to ridiculous levels.

The Pro needs to balance the line between features and price, while justifying its own existence. Otherwise, Samsung is just going to end up cannibalizing its own customer base and making the whole endeavor pointless.

Samsung has been an absolute demon for price hikes this year. Not only were multiple S26 models more expensive than their S25 counterparts, it also increased the price of the entire line-up back in September. To the point where the Galaxy S26 Ultra now costs $1,400. Officially, anyway, since the S26 series has been on sale almost everyday since.

Prices are high due to the skyrocketing cost of RAM and storage, and that means everyone has been hiking up the cost of their devices. With that in mind it would be really nice if Samsung didn't do that with the S27 series. Even if it's just a temporary reprieve, the last thing we need is phones getting even more expensive.

#3468. ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’s Most Terrifying Enemy Isn’t Inside the Dungeon

Dungeon Crawler Carl has completely taken over geek culture, which is impressive considering how hard it is to sum up the premise. The early novels take every big risk imaginable in a fantasy/science fiction story, and it does not make for a concise elevator pitch. However, even if you manage to break down this set up, the story evolves quickly to focus on much greater enemies outside the dungeon. This will be essential to understand when the TV adaptation premieres on Peacock, especially for new fans who may not realize what they're getting into. The show will have to balance the visual spectacle of the dungeon with the true story of Carl and his allies' secretive attempts to sabotage the game from within.

Dungeon Crawler Carl has come a long way from a serialized story self-published online to a best-selling novel series. Author Matt Dinniman has risen to the occasion at every step, coaxing the narrative to grow and evolve without straying too far from the wacky premise at its core. Still, it's been clear from the beginning that the dungeon itself is a sideshow, while humanity's real enemies are living amongst the stars. This balances well in the novels and makes for a fun, fast-paced adventure, but it may be difficult to bring to TV.

If you heard about Dungeon Crawler Carl via word of mouth, you probably got an elevator pitch something like this: Aliens take over earth and use advanced technology to instantly create a video game-like space inside the planet. Most humans are killed, and the survivors are encouraged to enter the dungeon to compete on an intergalactic game show called "Dungeon Crawler World." Awoken in the middle of the night, Carl enters with no shoes, not pants, and his ex-girlfriend's cat as his only companion. The dungeon makes his cat sentient and the two fight their way through the game in the hopes of surviving and restoring what they can of earth as they knew it.

That's all accurate, and it prioritizes what a new fan would need to know getting into the series without spoiling anything or focusing too much on details that will become important later. However, it could also give new fans some misinterpretations about the series. For one thing, recommendations like these tend to gloss over the fact that advanced aliens have been watching earth for thousands of years, and cultivating the planet to play this game one day. They gloss over the ancient technology already present on earth before the game began, and the tension between various alien factions as well as the System A.I. itself. It's true that these details aren't necessary at the beginning, but they become so integral later on that it can feel disingenuous to leave them out.

"There is some good in this world, Mr. Frodo... and it is worth fighting for."

Someone who actually picks up the Dungeon Crawler Carl novels will learn pretty quickly that the book isn't really about the game show itself. Carl and his allies look at the game only as a means of surviving, and they take every opportunity to undermine it for the viewers and the aliens involved. Ultimately, Carl's goal is to get the game shut down somehow and earn freedom for himself and the rest of the earthlings. It becomes a highly political story that some viewers might not be expecting, evoking themes of colonialism and violent uprising.

Meanwhile, the mystery of the alien technology is the central question of the series before long. To a newcomer, it's odd that this technology which is utilized for such an absurd, specific purpose can become a mystery later on, but in the context of the books it works beautifully. The question is whether the TV adaptation will pull it off as well — hopefully without softening the story's sharp edges in the process.

The best way for the TV adaptation to handle all of this confusion would be to broaden the audience's perspective early on. The books are written in the first person, and the audience learns about the worldbuilding and the conflicts at the same rate as Carl — more or less. However, adaptations often break out of this first-person perspective early on. It's harder to pull off in a visual medium, and it's difficult to disperse all the exposition needed from just one set of eyes.

Ideally, Peacock's adaptation will tease mysteries about the Borant Corporation, the various alien factions, and the System A.I. early on. If it needs to mix in scenes without Carl and Donut to do so, it will be worth it. The show has the luxury of looking ahead at what's important and interesting in the later books, and planting those ideas earlier than they were in the books. This is how adaptations get credit for strengthening their stories along the way.

For now, Dungeon Crawler Carl lives only on the page, and its transition to TV is a mystery on its own. There are eight novels available now in print, digital, and audiobook formats, with a ninth on the way and a tenth expected to finish the saga. Peacock's TV adaptation is in production now, but there's no word on when it may be released.

An easy reset to bring back sharp, natural picture quality

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Between toggling game mode on and off, turning on eye comfort shields for late-night viewing, and having native apps constantly override my display choices, my TV picture was looking, frankly, terrible.

It is easy to blame a poor streaming bit rate or assume the screen is wearing out, but usually it comes down to a mess of conflicting picture settings fighting each other in the background. After resetting my display and cutting out the clutter, I realized you do not need complicated calibration tools to get things looking right again.

Adjusting three specific settings sorted the issue out straight away, bringing back proper brightness, punchy contrast, and natural color.

The first thing holding your screen back is almost certainly an aggressive power-saving mode.

Most TVs ship with these turned on by default to meet regional energy efficiency rules, and they can sabotage your picture by capping backlight output or letting an ambient light sensor dim the screen the second you lower the lights in the evening.

Head into your TV’s general or picture settings menu, track down Eco Mode or Energy Saving, and switch it off.

Disabling it immediately unleashes the panel’s actual peak brightness, making highlights pop and finally giving HDR content the visual punch it is supposed to have.

If a prestige drama or big-budget action film looks less like cinema and more like a soap opera, motion smoothing is to blame. It's often labelled under names like TruMotion, Picture Clarity, or Motionflow.

The mechanism, however, is all the same: the TV artificially inserts fake frames between the real ones to force a hyper-smooth image. While that extra fluidity has its place in live sport, the unnatural effect ruins picture quality.

Dive into your picture or clarity settings, find the motion smoothing controls, and turn them off to restore that authentic, cinematic weight to your favourite films and shows.

Out of the box, most sets default to Standard or Vivid mode, which pushes harsh, overly blue whites and neon skin tones designed to catch your eye on a brightly lit shop floor. Swapping your primary preset to Filmmaker Mode or Cinema wipes out that artificial processing with a single press of the remote.

Filmmaker Mode disables heavy edge-sharpening filters, strips out fake contrast boosts, and sets the colour temperature to an accurate, industry-standard warm balance. It may look slightly yellow at first while your eyes adjust, but skin tones, shadows, and fine details will quickly look far more natural.

#3465. Hands-on time with the iPhone Duo still leaves me wowed

There are devices you need in your life, others for which you can put together a convincing justification – and then there are gadgets you quite simply want.

I said last month that I was wowed by the launch video for the iPhone Duo, despite it falling very clearly into the latter category for me – and playing with one hasn’t changed that in the slightest …

I had a very un-British reaction to the video for the new device.

I had extremely high expectations for this device yet was still blown away by just how good it appears to be. I’m British; the only time we ever use the word “wow” is sarcastically – but I still had to open this piece with it, without a trace of sarcasm.

This device isn’t the best match for me. To me, an iPhone is about 50% ultra-slim camera, 49% pocket computer, and 1% phone. The iPhone 18 Pro is a better device for my needs. However, I was experiencing extreme levels of technolust for the iPhone Duo. I’m not the target market for the iPhone Duo, but I do, absolutely, unquestionably want one.

I this week got a chance to visit an Apple store to spend about half an hour playing with the new device, and that did absolutely nothing to reduce my technolust.

The first thing to say is that the nanotexture surface of the inner display is gorgeous, and my quick snapshots don’t remotely do justice to it. Although intended primarily to disguise the crease, I found it a really beautiful screen. When looking at content with a white background, it’s really paper-like.

Indeed, once I’d been looking at it for a while, it was actually quite jarring to fold the Duo and see the glossy screen on the outside – all the more so when it showed reflections which were not at all visible on the inner display.

I honestly think Apple should have used nano-texture on the outer screen too, and even offer it as an option on other iPhones.

The iPhone Duo of course offers a split-screen view, with a new gesture to invoke it. Even in the very short time I was using the device, I found this almost immediately became second nature. From the home screen you simply drag an app up a little and then either left or right and it snaps into place.

Both apps feel very usable in this configuration, although in my view it would only make sense to use it when you are interacting with both, for example dragging content from one to another, like adding a photo to a note. I’m not much of a multi-tasker and, honestly, most people who claim to be aren’t either. For me the whole point of a phone display this size is greater immersion.

Most of the time, then, I’d want to take advantage of the iPad mini-like size of the display to give more space to a single app. For some content, like photos, it does rely on a matching aspect ratio to take full advantage of the display.

Other photo ratios get windowed, and look far less impressive.

For web browsing and similar applications, I would personally use it primarily in portrait mode.

Apple’s own apps seem well adapted to this mode. For example, the overlapping message pane in the Messages app, which can of course be dismissed.

For me, the least-convincing use case is watching video, where the aspect ratio simply doesn’t match most of today’s content. For example, this is how Foundation looks in the Apple TV app:

Incidentally, the camera punch hole looks very obvious above, but it really isn’t most of the time. With many backgrounds, it’s barely visible and not remotely intrusive. I had to angle the screen very carefully to be able to really maximise its visibility for this close-up:

I’d say it’s more visible in my other photos than it is in real-life.

Then there are the more whimsical orientations …

I have to say the touchscreen MacBook Pro is smaller than I expected pic.twitter.com/uLf4J3qjVi

Technolust: A perfect term to describe me and the Duo.

Like Ben, I was absolutely wow'd when I got hands on at the Apple Store. A Duo is in my future ... some day.

I mostly dictate text on an iPhone rather than type it, and can’t imagine anyone would really use the Duo in laptop mode very often, but honestly there’s nothing wrong with a bit of whimsy with the device. It’s in large part a fun thing – even if it is rather pricey as a toy.

The iPhone Duo is a beautiful device, and Apple has clearly put a huge amount of thought into both the hardware and the software.

It’s a very pocketable device, and I really love the idea of having a screen size close to that of the iPad mini on me at all times. I mentioned that I’d been using an iPad mini to preview the iPhone Duo experience earlier this month, and the Duo actually feels even better thanks to smaller bezels and that beautiful paper-like display.

Yes, it’s exceedingly expensive, and yes, having the priciest iPhone lack the best cameras would be a huge compromise for me. But while I still don’t think it would be the best iPhone for my needs, I do absolutely, undeniably want one.
